analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "May it please the Court, we have an agreement with counsel that petitioners will argue in number 10, and then we will reply in both 9 and 10 if that meets with the Court's approval. Mr. Chief Justice, may it please the Court, before this Court for review, upon the granting of a writ of certiorari, is the judgment of the Supreme Court of South Carolina affirming the convictions of petitioners for trespass. That law, Section 16386, by its terms, makes it a misdemeanor to enter upon the lands of another after notice from the owner or tenant prohibiting such entry. The Negro petitioners, in this case, are Columbia, South Carolina college students who were arrested on March 16, 1960, when they went into Eckerd's Drugstore, a large multi-department chain store, the only department of which, which is restricted to whites, is the lunch counter. The petitioners seated themselves in a booth in the lunch counter, and the owner asked them to leave, and the police officer asked them to leave, and after a few minutes' hesitation, one got up, the other was attempting to get up, and he was pulled up by the police officer. And they were arrested. Petitioners were tried in the recorders' court in the City of Columbia without a jury on March 25, 1960. They were convicted of trespass and sentenced to pay a fine of $100, $24.50, of which was suspended, or 30 days in jail. Their convictions were affirmed by the Richland County Court Criminal Division and by the Supreme Court of South Carolina. Throughout the state court proceedings, petitioners claimed that their arrests and convictions violated rights secured to them by the due process and equal protection clauses for the 14th Amendment to the Federal Constitution. Petitioners urged that their convictions amounted to state enforcement of private racial segregation to the use of the state's judicial machinery to enforce such discrimination in a public place where petitioners had been invited to trade and where they had the right to be, and that this action singled them out for different treatment by the state solely because of their race and color. These contentions were summarily overruled by the Supreme Court of South Carolina on the ground that similar contentions had been rejected by it in a similar case, the City of Greenville against Peterson, which was reversed here last term on other grounds. Upon this review, petitioners contend first that their rights have been violated because here the state's criminal law enforcement and judicial machinery were employed to sanction and enforce private racial discrimination in a place open to the public. Every member of the public could go into this place, and every white member of the public could sit at the lunch counter. Secondly, petitioners claim that their rights have been violated because the state is involved in this act of racial discrimination because it's an act performed by the manager of Eckert's Drugstore in obedience to a community-wide custom of racial segregation in public eating places, which custom in turn is dictated in part by state law and massively supported and encouraged by a network of corresponding state laws clearly defining that state's long-pursued policy of enforcing racial segregation not only in the public life of the state but in private affairs as well. Thirdly, petitioners claim that their rights have been violated because contrary to the command of the 14th Amendment that no state shall deny equal protection of the laws, South Carolina has denied same by a regime of laws which fails to furnish such protection to petitioners by subordinating petitioners' claim to equality in the public facilities of the community to a narrow and technical property claim which is no more than an assertion of a right to deny equal treatment to Negroes in one department of a store open to any member of the white public. Now, the gravamen of this case was put before the arresting officer in a single question which appears on page 17 of the record. The arresting officer was the assistant chief of police and he was asked this, Chief, isn't it a fact that the only reason you were called in from the police department to arrest these two persons was because they were Negroes who were asking for service in the food department of Eckerd's store and the manager was directing them out because they were Negroes. Isn't that correct? And the chief answered, Why, certainly. I would think that would be the case. Consequently, there is no question in this case that the policy of Eckerd's drugstore was to permit Negroes to trade in all of the numerous departments of the store except the lunch counter. At one point, the manager of the drugstore testified that he did not refuse to serve petitions because they were Negroes. That's on page 26. But when he realized that his previously admitted and obvious policy would not permit him under cross-examination to evade the crucial issue as to why service was denied, he asserted, All stores do the same thing. It is also clear that the manager's refusal to serve, therefore, was influenced by community custom, which we claim amounts to unconstitutional state action because dictated in part by state law and supported by a massive state segregation policy. Constitutionally relevant here is the fact that this community-wide custom of not serving Negro and white persons together in public eating places in South Carolina is expressly dictated in part by state law. At the turn of the century, when public eating places were largely the concern of people traveling, South Carolina made it a crime to furnish meals to white and colored persons in the same room, at the same table, or at the same counter, in station restaurants or station eating houses in times limited by common carriers of such passengers. And then, in Peterson versus City of Louisville, the case which was here last term, there was that South Carolina city ordinance in Greenville, which expressly required segregation and restrooms. In addition... There's no contention, is there, or is there, Ms. Motley, that any statute or ordinance directly bore on this situation here? No, sir, not. This statute, which I just referred to, referred to station restaurants and railroad stations. And you said... It did not say a lunch counter in a drug store. And that was the turn of the century, you told me. That's right. What I'm saying is that this is state policy, and this, the custom stemmed or was generated by this state policy expressed in this statute and numerous other state statutes, making the action of the owner the state action because it was so infused with state policy. But there was no, if I understand it correctly, there was no statute or ordinance which compelled this restaurant, this store proprietor to do as he did, to discriminate. That's right. There was no ordinance or state statute. And none which made it an offense for people to eat together. That's right. That's right. And as I've said, this custom, which was dictated in part by state law and that it expressed the state's policy with respect to public eating in a certain area, was again massively supported and has been for almost a century by South Carolina statutes which created the segregated society presently existing in that state because the state not only decreed segregation in the public life in facilities owned and operated by the state but in facilities owned and operated by private individuals as well. And as we point out in our brief, during Reconstruction, there's historical evidence that Negroes were able to eat in public eating places in Columbia, South Carolina, the same city involved here. And as late as 1895 and 1898, there was opposition in South Carolina to the enactment of racist legislation. However, it's obvious that the pro-segregation forces prevailed and after a brief, desegregated Reconstruction era, the policy of South Carolina changed and became that of segregation of the races, as we've said, as evidenced by these numerous laws which require segregation in such places as circuses and traveling shows, steam ferries, carrier station, restaurants, textile factories. In other words, the state extended its policy beyond the public life into private affairs. Well, may I ask, Mr. Botley, is your argument in essence this, that just as the store owner in Peterson would not be heard to say that he made a private choice in light of the existence of an ordinance expressly requiring segregated eating facility, here the store owner ought not be heard to say he made a private choice against the background or mosaic of segregation laws. That's right. Also, I didn't get to... Oh, yes. All of these that we've collected on page 28 of our brief, I think, footnote, it's page 30, footnote 11. We've collected all of the current laws in South Carolina bearing on segregation. Those require... Pardon me? Yes, sir. We filed a joint brief in 9, 10, and 12. Well, does this argument apply in 9 and 12 as well as in 10? It applies in, yes, in 9 and 10 and 12. Now, this may not be the appropriate place to ask that. Well, I think of it, Mrs. Botley. Are you also arguing the point that this South Carolina trustful statute does not give fair warning? Yes, we have argued that in our brief, and... Did you raise it in the... No, vagueness was not raised as such in the South Carolina court. However, throughout the proceeding, due process was raised, and when the case got to the Supreme Court in a petition for rehearing, it was expressly pointed out that free speech was involved, and one of these petitioners, Bowie, had been convicted of resisting arrest, and one of the assignments of error, or two of the assignments of error, were failure of the state to prove a prima facie case and failure of the state to prove a corpus delecti, which I understand in South Carolina means the state proved no crime, and that was raised and passed on by the Supreme Court of South Carolina, and they reversed Bowie's conviction for resisting arrest on the ground that there was no evidence to show that. So they did pass on the sufficiency of the evidence, and so here we're saying that there was no evidence to convict the petitioners of the crime defined by the statute. And you think that would embrace the fair warning point? Yes, that's right. Now, also relevant here, as I've just mentioned, is the fact that there has been no perceptible voluntary change in the state's policy. South Carolina announced, for example, just in August that it would close its state parks rather than desegregate them as required by a federal court. In other words, South Carolina is still pursuing and pushing a public policy of segregation. And this public policy permeates every aspect of life in South Carolina, either by direct legislative fire, as we've pointed out, or by public custom of the nature described here. Yes. In this case, I believe that after this case, Negroes were able to eat in this particular drugstore. Some Negroes have been admitted to state colleges, Clemson College, by court order, however, University of South Carolina, by court order, and Negro students were admitted to elementary schools in Charleston, South Carolina, in September pursuant to court order. Mr. Blum, the previous policy would still be there. Well, I think the state would have to certainly at least provide a remedy against such discrimination. And the state in every case thereafter would have the burden of proving that there was no state power still infecting the private action here. And if the state could prove that, then the state exonerates itself. But I think... the state would have to do that before they could start claiming that they were no longer involved here, because otherwise we claim that in every one of these cases they would have a heavy burden of proving that this man acted without any relation to the prior state's policy in discriminating against a Negro who went into the drug store. Well, you see, the northern states have all passed statutes giving us a remedy against such discrimination. And certainly in that situation you go in the state court and force that state law. So the state... pardon me? Well, we cite 30 statutes, state statutes prohibiting discrimination in public accommodations. Now, they don't cover every single public accommodation, but there the state would not have the same heavy burden that South Carolina has of showing that the state's policy is not operating here. and we say that in all these cases the state could not be heard to say that its massive policy of segregation had no effect whatsoever and that it never intended to enforce segregation in this kind of situation. But if you go beyond that, as I understood your answer to me, Mrs. Myler, your answer is that no one will be heard to say that the choice was a private choice as long as there exists this kind of massive body of legislation requiring segregation, wasn't that it? Yes, that's right. It's not what that hurts. The state will be heard to say, but rather the private individual will not be heard to say that when he asked Negroes to leave, this was a private choice of segregation to segregation to segregation Well, if in South Carolina tomorrow they should repeal all state laws on segregation and the onus discriminated against us the next day, we say the state still has the burden of showing that his action was without any reference whatsoever to the state's previous policy or this custom which we claim was generated and supported by state law. And we think that the day after the state repeals all its laws in South Carolina would certainly be too soon for us to say there's no state involvement at all here because the magic of repealing those statutes has wiped out all of the influence which the state policy previously had. Well, now, what I had in mind is that we are doing the text and the text and the text is that a issue to call your identity system? Well, what worse would... No, no, you don't have to decide that in this case. No. Pattern, something very similar to it is going to be before us in the next case fell against Maryland, isn't it? Well, yes, in Maryland, the state has passed a statute, but there we say it's again too soon for the state to say it was its policy did not influence the owner because as a matter of fact, the owner said that's the only reason I'm segregating. I would love to have here. And in Maryland, they've had a similar massive segregation policy. It's only recently that they've begun to change that policy. In that case, the burden is still on the state to show that that policy has not influenced the choice of the owner. As a matter of fact, in that case, the owner said it does. It's the only thing that influences my choice. How do you suggest that such proof be induced? You're suggesting, it seems to me, that the courts get pretty deeply into the realm of psychology. Each of us is motivated by a variety of factors, inherited, environmental. Each of us is motivated by the customs of those with whom he lives. These are all fairly subtle psychological considerations calling upon a discipline which does not deal in exactitude. Is that the kind of evidence you think? Well, I think the state would have to begin with its laws to point out that these segregation laws, any having to do with this particular facility, have been repealed by the state, are not enforced by the state, and the state has gone further and provided a remedy against such discrimination. And all of this kind of thing, I think, the state would have to prove. And, of course, the state would then have to show that this was, it's been many years since the state had any such laws, that it couldn't possibly have had the effect which we claim. we only asked that the state be charged with the normal and probable consequences of its acts. But after all that evidence was in, then maybe the defense could get a psychologist on a stand to say that everybody is motivated by a desire to be respected by his peer group and so on, and that the peer group of the community still held these deeply entrenched, even subconscious, opinions. Would that be enough to answer? Well, no, I don't think just the psychologists coming in and saying that's what you're getting into, isn't it? Well, I don't think so. I think that there is so much evidence in this case, for example, of the state's policy, that we don't have to get into that. The state has a heavy burden right now in this case with all of these laws which require segregation, and I think that it would be a long time before we get involved in that kind of situation in South Carolina where we would have difficulty in proving or the state would have difficulty in proving no state involvement and no effect of the state's policy in this kind of situation. yes, certainly slaves didn't have the right to go into anything. The slave didn't have any right which the white man or the state was bound to respect. And then during Reconstruction, as I pointed out briefly in South Carolina, they did have some rights. And then segregation was established as a matter of state law and state policy and everything became segregated. in South and your footnote in phase three. Seems to indicate that these statues were passed in 1962. Is that right? With reference to circuses, traveling shows? No, that's the codification date. They're old statues. Yes, these are old statues. But they were all reenacted or recodified by the slave action? Yes, they were all recodified in 1962 code. There's no statute that prohibits the eating places themselves from serving. No, sir. Just the one that I referred to, and that's in the 1962 code, which prohibits serving Negroes and whites in a station restaurant. That's still in the code. Was that first enacted in 1962, Mrs. Botley? No, sir. In 1906, I believe, we checked that, and it gives the history of the legislation in the code under the statute, and it indicates that it was first enacted in 1906, that particular statute. When it was reenacted, though, it was not extended, or enlarged. No, it wasn't. Were there how long of Negroes have been admitted at all to the places like this drugstore? I think right after this suit. No, I mean to the drugstore, not to the lunch counter or anything, but just to the drugstore proper. Well, I suppose since the drugstore was open, I'm not certain of that. I think that in all these situations, Negroes have always been permitted to buy at all of the counters except the eating counter. There never was a fake policy of segregation. And retail establishments generally. Well, what happens as a matter of fact is that the facilities in these department stores are segregated like the restrooms. And if they had a lunch counter, it was sometimes segregated, or Negroes excluded altogether. But they could buy at the merchandise counters generally without discrimination. They might have had to wait until all the white customers were waited on, something like that. But the policy in these department stores and drug stores is to segregate only the eating. This, again, was part of the custom not to eat with Negroes. I take it there's no specific evidence in the record of any causal connection between the exclusion and the state policy or customs. Yes, the owner said all stores do the same thing when we asked him, or when he was asked, did you refuse to serve these petitions because they were Negroes? He first said no, and then he said, well, everybody does the same thing, which to me says, this is the custom, that what I'm doing is what everybody does. But that's the extent of the evidence in that regard. Yes. And, of course, the other evidence is what this court can take judicial notice of, and that's all of these statutes of South Carolina. Mrs. Motley, the desegregation of Eckert's, is that the only one that's been desegregated, the lunch counter there? I think you told us that presently that lunch counter is desegregated. I can ask the state, maybe they know of other stores that have been desegregated. They have been. Generally in Columbia? Yes. Lunch counters, he says, not restaurants per set. I'd like to save the remaining time for rebuttal. Mr. Chief Justice, may it please the court. I am replying on behalf of the City of Columbia in both numbers 9 and 10, and would request that you consider all of my remarks addressed to both cases except when I specify otherwise. I would first like to direct the court's attention to the problems of vagueness and the convictions on the merits in these cases. It's our position that these cases are not defective for those reasons, for three reasons. First, that petitioners fail to properly raise and present the question of whether they were guilty of trespass at all before the state Supreme Court. Secondly, that they had actual notice of the owner's policy before they entered these stores and therefore were guilty under the statutes. And thirdly, that the question of whether a construction of refusal to leave after entry, whether such a construction would be vague, was never presented at all to the state Supreme Court. How's your third point, Dickerson, the first point? The first point is that they didn't properly brief and argue whether they were guilty of anything. The third point is that they didn't raise the question of the constitutionality of the construction that was rendered by the state court. In connection with the first point, our state Supreme Court has rules that most appellant courts have regarding the exceptions and questions presented which are designed to focus for the court what the question involved is. The questions and the exceptions in these cases simply said that the state failed to prove a prima facie case and to produce a corpus delecta. There was no spelling out what the error of the trial court was. In their briefs, which we have attached as an appendix to our brief, in the Barr case, the petitioners fully argued the question of state action. But when it came to the question of the conviction on the merits, they simply said that the argument under question one, which was a state action argument, would simply take care of question two, which was the question of whether they were guilty of anything. And our Supreme Court refused to reach the question. They said that under our rules, they had improperly raised it and wouldn't consider it. Now, in the Bowie case... As a matter of South Carolina law, has this statute, I'm talking now about 16-386, which begins by saying every entry upon the lands of another where any horse, mule, cow, hog, or any other livestock is pastured. Has that been consistently construed to apply to places like drugstores? There are no cases... Presumably there are not many horses or cows... There were no cases involving drugstores until the Charleston against Mitchell decision, which was decided by this court a few days before these cases were decided. And after these convictions? After these convictions, that's correct. Now, there is language in an old 1926 decision which indicates that a refusal to leave after notice would be a misdemeanor, but that's purely dictum. That case didn't involve a drugstores, it didn't involve a refusal to entry. It was simply a comment by the court, a refusal to leave. It was simply a court comment that there would be a misdemeanor. There are no other decisions on it. Of course, we... It had been applied mostly in rural type cases involving farmland. Quite often you get the question of whether there's been a shooting with a question of retreat as to whether the trespasser had a duty to get off the premises when requested to do so. That's correct. That's correct. That's correct. In the Bowie case, coming back to our point number one, the petitioners did brief fully the question of whether or not Bowie was guilty of resisting arrest. And our Supreme Court reversed on that. But when it came to this matter of whether he was guilty of trespass, again, they simply passed it over. And we submit that the question was not properly presented to our court. Now, if you conclude that it was, then it's our position that these people had actual notice before they entered these premises. Our statute says, in part, every entry after notice from the owner prohibiting such entry shall be a misdemeanor. And each of these cases, the petitioners testified they had been in these stores many times previously, trading in the other departments. One petitioner testified he had bought food at a lunch counter to take out. Also, these petitioners testified specifically that their purpose, their sole purpose in entering these stores was to be served food, not to buy food to take out, not to use the other departments. And the records as a whole show that their entry into these stores was a demonstration to protest the owner's policy of refusing to serve negligence. The next thing is, uh, to get the fortune of, but I understand the test is when he comes up to that to want. Trespass after notice. Notice is given to the person not coming. That's correct. What difference does it make to the part of the crime that he actually knew that he wanted? I thought the crime of being there, or going in after he was warned not to do so. Which seemed to me that the purpose of requiring the notice is to let him know that he's not warned. If he already knows... But the statute doesn't make that a crime, does it? If, on that basis... Well, but if the crime is, and I would think both elements are necessary, that he goes on it after he's been warned not to do so by the owner. Well, it's our position that by the owner's maintaining of this policy and by the fact that the petitioners knew it, this notice had been brought home to them before they entered the premises. Now, he had adverted to hell his... In his desire that, in general, people not appear to him, appear to a certain group, that he might change his mind. The statute, I must confess I'm impressed somewhat by my home state, the statute, like it, does me clearly to crime him going on with it after he's been warned not to do so. He's supposed to hear you all along that they didn't want him, but they didn't tell him not to. Can you stretch that to make it a crime? Well, that's our position. That's your argument? That's what our argument is. That is an acute issue in that point. That point, that's correct, sir. We feel that by his holding his store out in this matter for sufficient length of time, and these people admittedly know it, two of them testified they expected to be arrested when they went, that they had notice. That's our position. That's your position on the merits if we reach the merits. That's correct. But your preliminary position is that this was never raised in the court not before. Now, if you conclude that it was raised, and that my interpretation of the statute is wrong, then you reach this constitutional question of vagueness as to whether a refusal to leave after what you must find to be proper entry is unconstitutionally vague. Now, again... On your first point, will that make it necessary for us to examine the briefs before your Supreme Court, as we had to do in Wright v. Georgia, decide whether, in fact, the question had been raised? We felt you should examine it. We have to do the same thing. We think so, and we have printed them as a pen in our briefs so that you can do so. Yes. May I ask you this question about your law and that you go? Of course the Supreme Court had desired to consider that question. Even though they're not raised, they have the power to do so. They have the power, no question about it. This is a Supreme Court rule which they 99% of the time enforce. But as happened in the Bowie case, they have the power to look into it because in Bowie, on the same exceptions, they did reverse the conviction for resisting arrest. And the exceptions were just as vague. But it was argued in the brief. And the court had it before. Do you think that makes a difference in whether or not we should consider the point, even though they had chosen, for some reason not made clear, to refuse to pass on it although they had power to do so under the law? If you're going to find error on the part of the state court, we feel this should be taken into consideration in your decision as to whether to review it. Now coming to the question of vagueness, this wasn't raised at all in the briefs, in the exceptions, in the questions. And in particular, we'd like to call your attention to the petitions for rehearings in our state court. We have a typical procedure whereby after the Supreme Court's decision, counsel can file a petition for rehearing. These were filed in this case. The rule, if I may read to you, in part says, the petition must be filed stating particularly the points supposed to have been overlooked or misapprehended by the court. Now these petitions for rehearing were not only filed, of course, after the decisions in these cases. They were also filed after the decision in Charleston against Mitchell, which I believe is pending before you now, in which our court did so construe the statute to make it a trespass, to refuse to leave. So the precise, and counsel were the same in all cases. So counsel had notice of this case. And the petition, the points raised in the petitions for rehearing, which are contained in the record, make absolutely no reference to this question of vagus. And it's our position that this court, under your decisions, is without jurisdiction to reverse for on a ground which was not raised at all, it would be highly improper to do so. Am I right in thinking that is the case, that the situation, that if we did consider it in the other case, that the court did, happened to find with us, but refused to pass it on this because the court did not, the Supreme Court would have cut out Carolina, did not cut out Carolina, because for some reason it didn't want to, we'd have outstanding decision against one and for the other on precisely the same ground. I'm afraid I lost your honest question. As I understand, you say that there is another case in which your court waived it. Well, that case is one of the cases, it waived it as to the question of resisting arrest, but this was, this question, maybe I think I've been confused. I have said in my first point is it wasn't properly raised. Now, I think when you say a case doesn't prove, a state doesn't prove a prima facie case, that covers the world, so in a sense it was raised. And I think under those circumstances our court could, under its rules, go into the matter. But this question of vagueness was not raised at all. Could they have considered it despite that fact? Well, of course, I assume a court can consider anything. Could they have considered it when it was raised later? I believe, in the petitions for rehearing, they could have. They could have granted a rehearing. And did they present that question there? They did not mention it in the petition for rehearing. Did they present it later? As I understand it, it's never been presented until we got here. That is the question. I just want to understand that. That's it. It was never presented. I believe it first showed up in a petition for a writ of certiorari. It was the first time that this came up. It was really a opinion. Now, in this case, in the Barr case, they said, we're not going to consider it because the exceptions don't comply with our rules. In the Bowie case, they did comment, in one sentence, I believe, in the opinion, that in discussing the resisting arrest question, they said they're obviously guilty of trust. Period. Now, whether their theory was the theory I'm proposing that they had noticed before they went in or whether it was a refusal to enter, it's impossible to tell on the right. In short, it's our position that under the decisions of this court, it would be highly improper to rule that the lower court is in error on a ground which it never had the opportunity to consider. And we submit that that phase of the case should be far. validation for truthSt疫 Dy arcade uploaded live chart transferdoor landlord premiers If the court concluded that they had actual notice, then, of course, they would have been forewarned. Now, if the court concluded that that actual notice did not count, I mean, that you couldn't consider that, then you would be faced with the question of whether refusal to leave was, or that kind of construction was vague. But it's... Would there be any evidence of any kind, of a crime, that we could prove it that you would not ask? Well, they did refuse. You mean that you say that you will not, that the only way our statute can be construed is forewarned. Right. Well, the only evidence we have of that is their actual knowledge. Now, short of that, we have none. All right. Now, we say, if we were to say that that was not forewarned, is there any evidence of the case at all through a corpse of the court?
